summary: Describes how to use Frame Relay for framing PPP packets. It is on the standards track as a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: PPP is the protocol that lets two computers at the end of a direct link agree on settings and authenticate each other before sending data. This document describes how to run PPP over Frame Relay, a carrier service that delivers packets over virtual circuits, and how each end recognises a Frame Relay frame that belongs to PPP.

subtitle: How the Point-to-Point Protocol is carried inside Frame Relay frames, and how the two ends tell PPP apart from other traffic.

tldr.problem: PPP gives a link a set of useful facilities, including link control, network-layer control protocols, authentication and compression, but it was defined for ISO 3309 HDLC-like framing. Frame Relay uses a different framing, and the two cannot share a link.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a PPP encapsulation inside the Q.922 Frame Relay frame, with the NLPID and the PPP Protocol field identifying PPP traffic, and with in-band demultiplexing rules that tell the two ends when a frame belongs to PPP.
tldr.outcome: PPP can run over a Frame Relay virtual circuit configured as a point-to-point link, with its own configuration recommendations for the magic number, protocol field compression and the maximum receive unit.

sections.title: What This Document Describes
sections.content:
The Point-to-Point Protocol provides a standard method for transporting multi-protocol datagrams over point-to-point links. This document describes the use of Frame Relay for framing PPP encapsulated packets.

The specification is intended for implementations that want to use the facilities defined for PPP, such as the Link Control Protocol, Network-layer Control Protocols, authentication and compression. These capabilities require a point-to-point relationship between peers, and are not designed for multi-point or multi-access environments.

Frame Relay is a relative newcomer to the serial link community. Like X.25, the protocol was designed to provide virtual circuits for connections between stations attached to the same Frame Relay network. The improvement over X.25 is that Q.922 is restricted to delivery of packets, and dispenses with sequencing and flow control, simplifying the service immensely. PPP uses ISO 3309 HDLC as a basis for its framing.

When Frame Relay is configured as a point-to-point circuit, PPP can use Frame Relay as a framing mechanism, ignoring its other features. This is equivalent to the technique used to carry SNAP headers over Frame Relay.

At one time it had been hoped that PPP in HDLC-like frames and Frame Relay would co-exist on the same links. Unfortunately, the Q.922 method for expanding the address from 1 to 2 to 4 octets is not indistinguishable from the ISO 3309 method, due to the structure of its Data Link Connection Identifier subfields, so co-existence is precluded.
sections.plainLanguage: Frame Relay frames carry an address that grows in steps of one, two or four octets, and the steps look different from the ones used by HDLC-style framing. The two schemes therefore cannot share the same link, and PPP has to be carried on its own.

sections.title: Physical Layer Requirements
sections.content:
PPP treats Frame Relay framing as a bit-synchronous link. The link MUST be full-duplex, but MAY be either dedicated, meaning permanent, or switched.

PPP presents an octet interface to the physical layer. There is no provision for sub-octets to be supplied or accepted. PPP does not impose any restrictions regarding transmission rate, other than that of the particular Frame Relay interface.

Implementation of Frame Relay requires the provision of control signals, which indicate when the link has become connected or disconnected. These in turn provide the Up and Down events to the LCP state machine. Because PPP does not normally require the use of control signals, the failure of such signals MUST NOT affect correct operation of PPP.

The definition of various encodings is the responsibility of the DTE and DCE equipment in use, and is outside the scope of this specification. While PPP operates without regard to the underlying representation of the bit stream, Frame Relay requires NRZ encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The link has to run in both directions at once, and it may be a permanent line or a switched one. PPP hands the hardware whole octets at a time and does not care how the bits are represented on the wire, although Frame Relay requires a particular encoding.

sections.title: The Frame Format
sections.content:
This specification uses the principles, terminology and frame structure described in Multiprotocol Interconnect over Frame Relay. The purpose of the specification is not to document what is already standardized there; instead it gives a concise summary and points out the specific options and features used by PPP.

As described there, the Q.922 header address and control fields are combined with the Network Layer Protocol Identifier, which identifies the encapsulation that follows, and the fields are transmitted from left to right. The frame carries a flag octet, the Q.922 address, a control octet, an NLPID octet whose value identifies the PPP encapsulation, and then the PPP Protocol field. The PPP Protocol field and the following Information and Padding fields are described in the Point-to-Point Protocol encapsulation document.
sections.plainLanguage: Each Frame Relay frame gets one extra octet that says what kind of payload follows, and PPP puts its own protocol field after that. The rest of the frame is the ordinary Frame Relay address and control octets.

sections.title: Modifications to the Basic Frame
sections.content:
The Link Control Protocol can negotiate modifications to the basic frame structure. However, modified frames will always be clearly distinguishable from standard frames.

Address-and-Control-Field-Compression. Because the Address and Control field values are not constant, and are modified as the frame is transported by the network switching fabric, Address-and-Control-Field-Compression MUST NOT be negotiated.

Protocol-Field-Compression. Unlike PPP in HDLC-like framing, the Frame Relay framing does not align the Information field on a 32-bit boundary. Alignment to a 32-bit boundary occurs when the NLPID is removed and the Protocol field is compressed to a single octet. When this improves throughput, Protocol-Field-Compression SHOULD be negotiated.
sections.plainLanguage: PPP can normally shrink its two-byte protocol number to one byte, and on Frame Relay that also puts the payload back on a 32-bit boundary, which saves copying. The address and control octets cannot be compressed, because the network rewrites them as the frame crosses each switch.

sections.title: In-Band Protocol Demultiplexing
sections.content:
The PPP NLPID, whose value is CF in hex, and the PPP Protocol fields easily distinguish the PPP encapsulation from the other NLPID encapsulations. The joining of the PPP and NLPID number space has an added advantage, in that the LCP Protocol-Reject can be used to indicate NLPIDs that are not recognized, which can eliminate the black holes that occur when traffic is not supported.

For network-layer protocols that have no PPP Protocol assignment, or that have not yet been implemented under the PPP encapsulation, or that have not been successfully negotiated by a PPP NCP, another method of encapsulation defined for Frame Relay SHOULD be used.

Currently there are no conflicts between NLPID and PPP Protocol values. If a future implementation is configured to send an NLPID value that is the same as a compressed Protocol field, that Protocol field MUST NOT be sent compressed.

On reception, the first octet following the header is examined. If the octet is zero, it MUST be assumed that the packet is formatted according to the Frame Relay multiprotocol specification. PPP encapsulated packets always have a non-zero octet following the header. If the octet is not the PPP NLPID value, and Protocol-Field-Compression is enabled, and the associated NCP has been negotiated, then it is expected to be a compressed PPP Protocol value. Otherwise, it MUST be assumed that the packet is formatted according to the Frame Relay multiprotocol specification. The Protocol field value 0x00cf is not allowed, being reserved, to avoid ambiguity when Protocol-Field-Compression is enabled; the value MAY be treated as a PPP Protocol indicating that another PPP Protocol packet follows.

Initial LCP packets contain the sequence cf-c0-21 following the header. When a LCP Configure-Request packet is received and recognized, the PPP link enters the Link Establishment phase. The accidental connection of a link to feed a multipoint network or a multicast group SHOULD result in a misconfiguration indication, which can be detected by multiple responses to the LCP Configure-Request with the same Identifier, coming from different framing addresses.

Once PPP has entered the Link Establishment phase, packets with other NLPID values MUST NOT be sent, and on receipt such packets MUST be silently discarded, until the PPP link enters the Network-Layer Protocol phase. Once PPP has entered the Network-Layer Protocol phase and successfully negotiated a particular NCP for a PPP Protocol, if a frame arrives using another equivalent data encapsulation, the PPP link MUST re-enter the Link Establishment phase and send a new LCP Configure-Request. This prevents black holes that occur when the peer loses state. An implementation that requires PPP link configuration, and other PPP negotiated features such as authentication, MAY enter the Termination phase when configuration fails. Otherwise, when the Configure-Request sender reaches the Max-Configure limit, it MUST fall back to sending only frames encapsulated according to the Frame Relay multiprotocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Each end looks at the first octet after the Frame Relay header to decide what it has received. Zero means an ordinary Frame Relay payload; the PPP marker means PPP; anything else is either a compressed PPP protocol number or an ordinary payload, depending on what was negotiated. If a peer starts sending the wrong kind of frame, the link renegotiates rather than carrying traffic into a hole.

sections.title: Out-of-Band Signalling
sections.content: There is no generally agreed method of out-of-band signalling. Until such a method is universally available, an implementation MUST use In-Band Protocol Demultiplexing for both Permanent and Switched Virtual Circuits.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no separate signal on the wire that says a virtual circuit is carrying PPP, so the ends have to work it out from the packets themselves. This holds for both permanent and switched circuits.

sections.title: Configuration Details
sections.content:
The document recommends the Magic Number and Protocol Field Compression configuration options, and says that the standard LCP configuration defaults apply to Frame Relay links except for the Maximum-Receive-Unit.

To ensure interoperability with existing Frame Relay implementations, the initial MRU is 1600 octets. This affects only the minimum required buffer space available for receiving packets, not the size of packets sent. The typical network feeding the link is likely to have an MRU of either 1500, or 2048 or greater, so to avoid fragmentation the Maximum-Transmission-Unit at the network layer SHOULD NOT exceed 1500, unless a peer MRU of 2048 or greater is specifically negotiated.

Some Frame Relay switches are only capable of 262 octet frames. It is not recommended that anyone deploy or use a switch which is capable of less than 1600 octet frames. However, PPP implementations MUST be configurable to limit the size of LCP packets which are sent to 259 octets, which leaves room for the NLPID and Protocol fields, until LCP negotiation is complete.

XID negotiation is not required to be supported for links which are capable of PPP negotiation, and Inverse ARP is not required to be supported for PPP links, because that function is provided by PPP NCP negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the two ends have agreed anything, they may still be using a small Frame Relay switch, so the link setup packets have to be kept small. Once the link is up, the receive buffer is set to 1600 octets, and the network layer is told not to send packets larger than 1500 unless both ends have negotiated a larger one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The document says that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The facilities it relies on for authentication are those of PPP itself, described in the Point-to-Point Protocol document.
sections.plainLanguage: This document says nothing about security. The authentication it can offer is the authentication PPP already provides, not anything new.

fields.desc: Identifies the encapsulation that follows; 0xcf marks PPP.

viz.caption: READING THE FIRST OCTET AFTER THE FRAME RELAY HEADER

items.title: The octet is zero
items.text: The packet is formatted as an ordinary Frame Relay multiprotocol payload.

items.title: Anything else
items.text: A compressed PPP Protocol value, if compression is enabled and the NCP was negotiated; otherwise an ordinary Frame Relay payload.

items.title: The value 0x00cf
items.text: Reserved, to avoid ambiguity when protocol field compression is enabled.

items.title: cf-c0-21
items.text: The sequence that follows the header in initial LCP packets; recognising it starts link establishment.

items.title: Initial MRU
items.text: 1600 octets, the minimum receive buffer, for interoperability with existing Frame Relay implementations.

items.title: Network-layer MTU
items.text: Should not exceed 1500 unless a peer MRU of 2048 or greater is negotiated.

items.title: LCP packet size
items.text: Must be configurable to 259 octets, which leaves room for the NLPID and Protocol fields.

items.title: XID and Inverse ARP
items.text: Not required to be supported, because PPP negotiation provides those functions.
